claims.text: DFT-based simulations can predict stable three-dimensional nanoframeworks of noble-metal-based high-entropy alloys.
DFT-based simulations can be used to design stable NM-HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
DFT can identify optimal NM-HEA compositions.
DFT can identify synthesis conditions that overcome challenges associated with diverse compositions and complex surface structures.
Temperature, pressure, and noble-metal ratios are relevant variables for the proposed nanoscale simulations.
DFT predicts stable nanostructures by minimizing energy.
DFT predicts stable nanostructures by optimizing atomic arrangements.
DFT-guided NM-HEA nanoframeworks will have 20% greater stability than nanoframeworks made by traditional synthesis methods.
The proposed stability improvement can be measured using cohesive energy per atom in eV/atom.
The complexity of NM-HEAs may limit the predictive accuracy of DFT simulations.
Available computational resources may limit the predictive accuracy of DFT simulations.
TEM or XRD can be used to characterize the structures of the resulting nanoframeworks.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention describe DFT as a computational prediction and design method, whereas the experiment refers to nanoframeworks as being physically 'produced using DFT-based simulations.' DFT alone does not constitute a physical synthesis route.

The predicted outcome specifies a 20% stability increase, but the hypothesis is only falsified below 15%; an observed 15–19% increase would fail to achieve the stated prediction without falsifying it.
